Thus Czechoslovakia at 17,000 was smaller than Poland, Hungary, Romania, France, Germany, Italy, Austria (18,000) and others, not larger than most. It also says, 'upon information and belief', that a material portion of other FTX transfers to CFAR funded Lightcone and the acquisition and renovation of the property (https://forum.effectivealtruism.org/posts/YSuqwrXFtuXuSzGDc/linkpost-sam-bankman-fried-funded-a-group-with-racist-ties; https://www.sfgate.com/tech/article/sbf-berkeley-rose-garden-inn-19520351.php).

Why the claim fails:
- The deposit went to a title company, not to CFAR. These were allegations in a complaint, not findings.
- Lightcone CEO Oliver Habryka said no FTX funds were used in buying Lighthaven. He guessed the $1M deposit is still sitting with the escrow company, which has been trying to return it to FTX (https://protos.com/ftx-chasing-5m-spent-on-right-wing-conference-venue/; https://www.sfgate.com/tech/article/sbf-berkeley-rose-garden-inn-19520351.php).

- Lightcone later settled with the FTX estate. The settlement was funded by Tallinn and the Survival and Flourishing Corp. (SFC) with about $1.7M (https://grantmaking.aisafety.com/projects/eca9804a-7673-4be8-837e-1c75b141781c).
- The wires went out in July and August 2022. FTX collapsed in November 2022, so 'as it was collapsing' is imprecise.

FTX money did flow to CFAR and Lightcone in 2022, and the estate alleged some of it went toward the property. The claim goes further than that. It states as settled fact that the property was bought with money wired to CFAR, and the evidence contradicts that.

cascade.findings: Claim is well-supported by labor history sources and is not misleading. The AFL was founded in 1886 as a loose federation of craft unions under Samuel Gompers, dedicated to principles of craft unionism https://www.britannica.com/topic/AFL-CIO . Its approximately 100 national and international unions retained full autonomy and each received "exclusive jurisdiction" over a craft, with "one union per craft; one craft per union," which produced bitter jurisdictional disputes between affiliates https://www.britannica.com/topic/AFL-CIO . Craft unions are described as organizing by specific craft/trade (e.g., all carpenters in carpenters' union, plasterers in plasterers' union) with own administration, agreements and halls https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Craft_unionism . Coming out of guild tradition, they policed how work was done by "maintaining standards for admission into the trade; requiring entrants to go through an apprenticeship program controlled by the union, rather than the employer; and dictating the processes, tools, standards, and pace of work" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Craft_unionism . Related summaries note membership was exclusive to those with particular skills to maintain strong control over labor supply in specialized areas, limiting membership to skilled workers and excluding unskilled workers, with craft exclusivity creating barriers to entry https://www.britannica.com/topic/AFL-CIO https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Craft_unionism . AFL unions required union members only via closed shop and "Selective admission to apprenticeships restricted membership, thereby artificially limiting the supply of skilled labor" is the standard textbook description of early trade-union control.

samples.research:
Rovell's 9.5% figure for Knicks-Spurs checks out as an internally consistent calculation: ESPN/NBA reported that Game 5 of the 2026 Finals "averaged 24.5 million viewers and peaked at 33 million viewers" (https://sports.yahoo.com/articles/knicks-thrilling-nba-finals-most-223739085.html, https://x.com/NBAPR/status/2066994469178605783). 33 million divided by the 2026 US population (~345-347 million) yields almost exactly 9.5%.

However, the 26.1% figure for the 1998 Bulls-Jazz series uses a different and non-comparable metric. The actual peak *simultaneous* audience for the highest-rated game of that series (Game 6) was an average of 35.89 million viewers with a 22.3 household rating/38 share (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBA_Finals_television_ratings, https://www.basketballinsiders.com/news/nba-finals-ratings-history-2000-present/). That figure, divided by the 1998 US population (~270 million), yields about 13.3% — not 26.1%. The 26.1% number appears to be derived instead from NBC's separate estimate that '72 million people watched all or part of' Game 6 (https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/lifestyle/1998/06/17/bulls-a-winner-for-nbc/9e4ac4dd-ecb0-4aa8-b6fd-a6f6e56535a6/, also cited on Grokipedia). That 'watched all or part of the broadcast' figure is a cumulative/reach metric counting everyone who tuned in for any portion of the 3+ hour broadcast, which is always much larger than the simultaneous peak audience (just as the Knicks-Spurs series also had a far larger cumulative reach than its 33-million peak).

So the tweet compares two fundamentally different measurements — a 'peak simultaneous audience' stat for 2026 (9.5%) against a 'cumulative total reach' stat for 1998 (26.1%) — which inflates the apparent gap between the two events. Using comparable peak-simultaneous-viewer metrics, the 1998 Bulls-Jazz Game 6 was about 13% of the population, versus about 9.5% for Knicks-Spurs Game 5 — a real but much smaller gap than the 9.5% vs 26.1% comparison implies.

The reply's claim — that Steam itself enforces mandatory DRM requiring reauthentication every 30 days, and that 'your games will break in 30 days once Steam goes down' — is partially true but overstated and imprecise. There IS a real offline-mode reauthentication mechanism in the Steam client, but the exact time window is inconsistent across sources and not fixed at 30 days: some report 14-30 days (https://gamewiki.blog/what-happens-if-i-play-steam-games-offline), some report 7-10 days (https://theportablegamer.com/2026/03/25/how-to-go-offline-on-steam-complete-guide-to-invisible-mode-offline-play-in-2026/), others 2 weeks (https://steamcommunity.com/discussions/forum/0/2798376078346605932), and one Steam Discussions poster states 'This 2 week limitation used to apply to all games on Steam, but was patched out of Steam's client-side DRM in ~2013' (https://steamcommunity.com/discussions/forum/0/2798376078346605932), implying the reauthentication requirement for pure Steam-DRM games (without Denuvo/third-party DRM) may no longer be a fixed timer at all. A Steam forum answer states 'if a game has Steam DRM on it, and only Steam DRM with no Denuvo or any other 3rd party DRM, then it can last indefinetly' offline, barring forced updates (https://steamcommunity.com/discussions/forum/0/1744483505475893224).

Crucially, the reply conflates the Steam client-level login/offline-mode mechanism with per-game DRM and claims ALL Steam games 'will break in 30 days once Steam goes down.' This is false for the subset of games that are genuinely DRM-free on Steam — as one source notes, Steam DRM-free games 'can be copied out of the Steam folder and run anywhere' (https://tech-insider.org/steam-vs-gog-2026/), and these function essentially like GOG installers, unaffected by any reauthentication timer. Thus the reply's blanket claim overgeneralizes and is not fully accurate, though it correctly identifies that Steam's client imposes some periodic reauthentication for games that do rely on Steam DRM/client — a nuance the original quoted post (which said DRM is optional and dev-controlled) did not directly address or dispute.

Overall: the exchange is mostly a dispute over nuance rather than a clear factual error that misleads readers in a consequential way. Both posts contain partially true but incomplete framing; neither is flatly false in a way likely to mislead on a major point, since Steam offline-reauthentication is real (though timing is disputed/not officially published by Valve), and DRM-free Steam games genuinely exist and work like GOG files.

UK's Debt Respite Scheme (Breathing Space) only 'provides temporary relief from enforcement action and interest charges for individuals undergoing mental health crisis treatment' https://themoneyknowhow.com/can-debt-be-written-off-due-to-mental-health/ , specifically 'temporary immunity from enforcement action and interest charges for the duration of their treatment... even though its purpose is to offer relief rather than debt forgiveness' https://themoneyknowhow.com/can-debt-be-written-off-due-to-mental-health/ , and 'Total debt write-off remains rare' requiring 'difficult procedure requiring financial and legal advice' https://themoneyknowhow.com/can-debt-be-written-off-due-to-mental-health/ . Contracts signed while medicated/mentally impaired are 'generally voidable, not automatically void. That means the law does not erase it on its own; you have to challenge it' https://getoutofdebt.org/269757/signed-debt-while-medicated-pressured-do-i-still-owe-it , 'A voidable contract is fully enforceable unless and until the impaired party takes action to avoid it. Nobody erases it for you' https://getoutofdebt.org/269757/signed-debt-while-medicated-pressured-do-i-still-owe-it , and 'It's voidable, not void. Nothing happens automatically' https://getoutofdebt.org/269757/signed-debt-while-medicated-pressured-do-i-still-owe-it . Author appears South African; South Africa also has no mental-hospital cancellation - discharge requires formal sequestration court order, while alternatives are 'debt review in terms of the National Credit Act 34 of 2005 or administration orders in terms of the Magistrates' Court Act 32 of 1944' https://journals.assaf.org.za/index.php/per/article/view/13539 , and prescription only after prolonged non-payment/acknowledgement, not hospitalization. Claim reverses reality: hospitalization typically adds medical bills and lost income, leaving 'The debt will still be there to deal with once you're safe' https://getoutofdebt.org/244812/mental-health-crisis-debt-what-can-i-do .

samples.research: The claim in the post is a widely circulated internet legend about cornrows being used by slaves to map escape routes and store food. Snopes investigated this twice (2022 and May 2026) and found no solid documentation for the claim as applied to U.S. slavery specifically: researchers found no tangible evidence of slaves in the U.S. using cornrows to convey escape messages (https://www.snopes.com/news/2022/03/12/maps-cornrows-black-slaves-escape/, https://www.snopes.com/news/2026/05/16/slaves-braided-maps-cornrows/). The origin story is most documented in Colombia, tied to a 17th-century figure named Benkos Bioho who built a maroon village and reportedly had women encode escape maps/messages in cornrows (https://www.snopes.com/news/2022/03/12/maps-cornrows-black-slaves-escape/, https://www.ancient-origins.net/weird-facts/braids-0017595) — this is a Colombian/South American oral tradition, not a documented U.S. slavery practice, despite the post's framing of 'runaway slaves' (commonly understood in U.S. context). Experts describe these as oral legends/urban legends serving symbolic/emotional functions rather than verified historical fact, comparable to the debunked 'quilt code' Underground Railroad myth (https://www.snopes.com/news/2022/03/12/maps-cornrows-black-slaves-escape/, https://www.truthorfiction.com/did-slaves-braid-routes-to-freedom-into-hairstyles/). The seed/food-storage claim has somewhat more academic grounding via geographer Judith Carney's book 'Black Rice,' which recounts a Suriname maroon oral tradition about rice seeds smuggled in hair, but this is also presented as legend/oral history rather than confirmed documented fact, and relates to the Middle Passage/maroon communities in South America rather than U.S. runaway slaves escaping via established routes (https://www.snopes.com/news/2026/05/16/slaves-braided-maps-cornrows/, https://face2faceafrica.com/article/how-hair-was-used-to-smuggle-grains-into-the-caribbean-by-african-slaves). Overall, this is a commonly repeated but unverified/mythologized claim lacking primary historical documentation, and fact-checkers have consistently rated it as unproven or false when presented as documented history rather than folklore.

Did you know cornrows were used by runaway slaves to map escape routes, as well as store food for their journey

## Research findings

The claim in the post is a widely circulated internet legend about cornrows being used by slaves to map escape routes and store food. Snopes investigated this twice (2022 and May 2026) and found no solid documentation for the claim as applied to U.S. slavery specifically: researchers found no tangible evidence of slaves in the U.S. using cornrows to convey escape messages (https://www.snopes.com/news/2022/03/12/maps-cornrows-black-slaves-escape/, https://www.snopes.com/news/2026/05/16/slaves-braided-maps-cornrows/). The origin story is most documented in Colombia, tied to a 17th-century figure named Benkos Bioho who built a maroon village and reportedly had women encode escape maps/messages in cornrows (https://www.snopes.com/news/2022/03/12/maps-cornrows-black-slaves-escape/, https://www.ancient-origins.net/weird-facts/braids-0017595) — this is a Colombian/South American oral tradition, not a documented U.S. slavery practice, despite the post's framing of 'runaway slaves' (commonly understood in U.S. context). Experts describe these as oral legends/urban legends serving symbolic/emotional functions rather than verified historical fact, comparable to the debunked 'quilt code' Underground Railroad myth (https://www.snopes.com/news/2022/03/12/maps-cornrows-black-slaves-escape/, https://www.truthorfiction.com/did-slaves-braid-routes-to-freedom-into-hairstyles/). The seed/food-storage claim has somewhat more academic grounding via geographer Judith Carney's book 'Black Rice,' which recounts a Suriname maroon oral tradition about rice seeds smuggled in hair, but this is also presented as legend/oral history rather than confirmed documented fact, and relates to the Middle Passage/maroon communities in South America rather than U.S. runaway slaves escaping via established routes (https://www.snopes.com/news/2026/05/16/slaves-braided-maps-cornrows/, https://face2faceafrica.com/article/how-hair-was-used-to-smuggle-grains-into-the-caribbean-by-african-slaves). Overall, this is a commonly repeated but unverified/mythologized claim lacking primary historical documentation, and fact-checkers have consistently rated it as unproven or false when presented as documented history rather than folklore.
